newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr dips after Greenspan talks on rates.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr dips after Greenspan talks on rates.

text.p: The Australian dollar slipped below US$0.7800 late in morning trading after a speech by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan drew varied interpretations on the outlook for U.S. rates.

Some felt Greenspan indicated rates would rise in May and others felt rates would be on hold after the May 20 FOMC meeting. The reaction of a weaker Australian dollar suggested the May rate hike view had prevailed, at least initially.
By noon (0200 GMT), the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7774/79, down on an early US$0.7807/12 and almost level with a local close on Thursday of US$0.7776/81.

The local dollar had spent most of the morning above US$0.7800 after strengthening on Thursday offshore, but the prospect of higher U.S. rates was a negative for the unit, even though traders said talk of a U.S. rate hike in May was not new.
"I think people have been aware of this May 20 rate hike for some time -- I'm surprised they're surprised," one trader said of the markets reaction to Greenspans speech.

There was also some Aussie/yen selling in late morning which added to the weaker tone traders said. By noon the Australian dollar was at 95.69/79 yen, well down on an early 96.69/79 and a local close of 97.08/18.
In trade weighted terms, the dollar had slipped to 60.0 from an opening 60.3 and an close of 60.2.

Greenspan said the Fed would need to act if growth failed to slow as expected, and the economy had little slack now. He saw scant signs of an imminent inflation resurgence, and while modest growth and low inflation was still likely in 1997/98, it was less sure now.

While some interpreted those as suggesting another pre-emptive move was likely, they were also seen by others as suggesting rates would remain steady after May, as the Fed was still assessing the strength of the economy.
Greenspan defended the March rate hike against what he said was an unusual amount of critcism, and said 1997 was not like 1994 when rates had to be raised sharply to head off inflation.
Like the interpretation of what Greenspan said, the U.S. dollar reaction was mixed.

The dollar had extended its weaker tone of this week ahead of the speech, but after intially rising on the comments, shortly before 0200 GMT the dollar dropped below 123 yen for the first time in a month as the market remained wary of central bank intervention and fears the Japanese government would talk up a stronger yen.
Traders said despite the weakness of the U.S. dollar, the prospect of higher U.S. rates and the yen selling against the Australian dollar, the local unit should not fall too much further.
"I don't think its going to fall out of bed necessarily from here, I think it's getting to a level where you'll see some stability," the trader said, nominating key support at around US$0.7730/40.
